title: Newton Hit by an Apple? In 1726 He Said It Just Fell｜Curio Archive
description:
Did an apple hit Newton on the head and give him gravity? The scene has been retold for almost 300 years, yet nobody who heard Newton tell it wrote it that way.
For anyone who grew up with this story and wants to know where it really came from.

On April 15, 1726, the doctor William Stukeley had tea with 83-year-old Newton under apple trees in London, and Newton brought up that apple. Stukeley wrote it into his 1752 memoir manuscript, which then went unprinted for 184 years. Voltaire, John Conduitt (husband of Newton's niece) and Henry Pemberton, who edited Newton's Principia, each left a different version, and Newton's own late note talks about the Moon instead. So who first wrote "hit on the head", and how did it reach the textbooks? This episode lays out every record in order, then visits the old apple tree at Woolsthorpe that still blossoms today.

Some things the records cannot settle: Voltaire's line that Newton's niece told him the story was added only in an edition more than ten years later; "earliest" means the earliest found so far; accounts differ on when the tree blew down, and there is no evidence Newton pointed it out himself. Sources are listed below.

t001.text: You've heard it: apple hits Newton's head, then gravity.

t002.text: Storybooks, textbooks: you likely heard it too.

t003.text: But those who heard it from Newton? None wrote the apple hit his head.

t004.text: Stranger: Newton's own notes on gravity talk about the moon.

t005.text: The earliest 'hit on the head' we can find: an anonymous pamphlet.

t005b.text: And the record closest to Newton's own words sat unprinted for 184 years.

t006.text: Today: did that apple hit Newton's head?

t007.text: I'm a Bureau researcher. Back to Newton's early 20s.

t008.text: Newton: born Christmas 1642, in rural Lincolnshire.

t009.text: This dark tricorn hat stands for Newton.

t010.text: Later he studied at Cambridge. In 1665, plague shut it down.

t011.text: He went home to the country, aged 23 or 24.

t012.text: Nearly two years in all; Cambridge reopened a few months.

t013.text: The garden had an apple tree. Keep it in mind.

t014.text: Later, Newton wrote of those years in a note. What did it say?

t015.text: Late in life, he listed there what he'd found when young:

t016.text: series, tangents, up to light's colors.

t017.text: Of 1666, he wrote: that year, I began to wonder if gravity reached the moon.

t018.text: Between the lines: all in the two plague years.

t019.text: The note has the moon, no apple. No apple in Newton's hand is known yet.

t020.text: So who first told of this apple?

t021.text: The earliest we can find: Newton, at 83, telling a doctor. His name: Stukeley.

t022.text: In 1721, Stukeley had visited Newton's birthplace.

t023.text: Why did his notes skip the apple tree?

t024.text: Wait: the tree's researcher guesses he may not have heard the story yet.

t026.text: Warm day; after dinner, tea under the apple trees, alone.

t027.text: Newton said gravity came to him just like this: an apple fell.

t028.text: Oddly, Stukeley's diary logs the visit but not a word of apples.

t029.text: Diary: April 15, dined alone with him at Kensington.

t030.text: The tree's researcher quoted it in a paper. So where's the apple?

t031.text: In his 1752 memoir manuscript, now at the Royal Society.

t032.text: It adds detail: that time, he sat deep in thought.

t033.text: He thought: why do apples always fall straight down?

t034.text: Not sideways, not up, but always to Earth's center?

t035.text: His answer: Earth pulls it. Matter must hold a pull,

t036.text: in proportion to its quantity. So the apple pulls Earth too.

t037.text: The closest record we have to Newton's words; still, Stukeley's retelling.

t038.text: Where? When? Did it touch him?

t039.text: None of the three: no place, no year, just 'formerly';

t040.text: no word of it hitting his head. The apple appears only here.

t041.text: Listen again: the manuscript says it 'fell.'

t043.text: A 184-year gap. By then, others had long spread the apple story.

t044.text: But was Stukeley the only one to write it down?

t045.text: No. In 1727, when Newton died, an English book

t046.text: had the apple. Its author, Voltaire, was in England when Newton died.

t047.text: He wrote: on a garden walk, Newton saw an apple fall,

t048.text: and had his first idea of gravity. Walking now, not sitting.

t049.text: This book doesn't say. So who told Voltaire?

t050.text: In 1741, in a new edition of another book, he added:

t051.text: 'His niece told me.' She kept house for him.

t052.text: One day in the country, Newton saw fruit fall from a tree, and mused.

t053.text: Note: it says 'fruit.' Not even an apple.

t054.text: Who else in the family wrote it?

t055.text: Her husband Conduitt was his Mint deputy.

t056.text: After Newton died, he drafted a biography.

t057.text: One: musing in a garden on the force that drops apples;

t058.text: another: an apple falling from a tree. When?

t060.text: Remember? 'All in the two plague years.' Newton claimed both.

t061.text: Either way, none say it hit his head.

t062.text: Notice? As it spread, Newton's pose changed: sitting, walking. A third's coming.

t063.text: Also: Pemberton edited the Principia's 3rd edition.

t064.text: He asked Newton how the theory arose. Apple in his book?

t065.text: In 1728 he published a book on Newton; its preface: Newton sat alone in a garden,

t066.text: pondering gravity: why not up to the moon? he asked.

t067.text: A garden, the moon, but no apple. That matters soon.

t069.text: In that pamphlet. First edition: London, 1739,

t070.text: no mention of Newton; author still unknown.

t071.text: Then the second edition, c. 1740, added this:

t072.text: His gravity hint: an apple on his head as he sat under a tree.

t073.text: It adds: but he had to be a mathematician;

t074.text: or a whole orchard falling would just feel heavy, hard.

t075.text: That one made me laugh. Here the apple finally hits a head.

t076.text: Says who? The book says: Pemberton.

t077.text: Pemberton's book? A garden, the moon, no apple.

t078.text: Only this pamphlet has the head hit?

t079.text: A letter: September 1760, Euler wrote a German princess on Newton.

t080.text: It says: the great English philosopher-mathematician lay one day under an apple tree,

t081.text: and an apple fell on his head. Remember the third pose?

t082.text: This is it: lying down. Sitting, walking, lying: all three.

t083.text: Euler: yet the moon didn't fall on his head;

t084.text: so he guessed its motion kept the moon up.

t085.text: Had the apple missed his head, we might still not know.

t086.text: How far? In 1768 they became a book;

t087.text: the 1795 English one says the same.

t088.text: But did every reader believe it?

t089.text: A Paris editor noted: likelier than an apple is Newton's 'by thinking on it.'

t090.text: Doubts aside, by the 1800s the head hit was usual.

t092.text: Anyone else would eat it, not ponder gravity.

t094.text: It's not over. Just then, one man dared not put the apple in his text.

t096.text: Its note: no source for the apple story, so he dared not use it.

t097.text: Over 20 years later, he put it back: Newton's niece told Voltaire.

t098.text: Paper spread the apple; the ground has a tree. Recall Newton's garden tree?

t099.text: When was it first called 'the one'?

t100.text: The earliest record, an 1806 local history: the tree still stood,

t101.text: shown to visitors. Newton: dead nearly 80 years.

t102.text: Over 60 years after the head-hit pamphlet. Did Newton pick the tree?

t103.text: No proof. Its researcher thinks it was chosen

t104.text: as the garden's only apple tree.

t105.text: Stukeley's 1721 record? No tree either. What became of it?

t107.text: Its writer: in his father's boyhood, a gale one night; next day, word Newton's tree fell.

t108.text: A teacher took pupils there to saw off lengths of branch.

t109.text: But the fallen trunk rooted again; it still blooms and fruits at the manor.

t110.text: You'd see an old tree from a fallen trunk, in a low fence.

t111.text: So, our opener: did the apple hit Newton's head?

t112.text: First, another: did it really show him gravity?

t113.text: No verdict; scholars split. Some demote it to unbacked anecdote;

t114.text: the tree's researcher: Newton wouldn't risk his soul on a needless lie.

t115.text: Historians, too: recalling 60 years back, old Newton may have built a legend.

t116.text: So the head part closes: the apple's on record; the head hit came later.

t117.text: Hear 'apple hits head' again? Recall the tea: Newton only said it fell.

t118.text: Each retelling adds detail. Vivid bits? Ask: who added that?

t119.text: Tell me: in your version, did it hit his head?
